171: This page features two inspirational quotes in large text. The first states: 'Riches do not respond to wishes. They respond only to definite plans, backed by definite desires, through constant PERSISTENCE.' The second states: 'EVERY FAILURE BRINGS WITH IT THE SEED OF AN EQUIVALENT SUCCESS.' These quotes serve as a thematic divider between Chapter 7 (Decision) and Chapter 8 (Persistence), encapsulating core principles: that wealth follows definite plans and persistent effort rather than mere wishing, and that failure itself contains the potential for equivalent success. The page bears the OceanofPDF.com watermark.
172: This page opens Chapter 8: PERSISTENCE—The Sustained Effort Necessary to Induce Faith (The Eighth Step to Riches). Hill states PERSISTENCE is essential in transmuting DESIRE into its monetary equivalent, and its basis is the POWER OF WILL. Willpower and desire combined make an irresistible pair. People who accumulate great fortunes are often thought cold-blooded and ruthless, but they are misunderstood—they have willpower mixed with PERSISTENCE placed behind their desires. Henry Ford was misunderstood as ruthless because of his habit of following through all plans with PERSISTENCE. The majority throw aims overboard at the first sign of opposition or misfortune; a few carry on DESPITE all opposition until they attain their goal—these are the Fords, Carnegies, Rockefellers, and Edisons. There may be no heroic connotation to 'persistence,' but the quality is to character what carbon is to steel. Building a fortune generally involves applying all 13 principles with PERSISTENCE.
173: Hill tells readers their first test of PERSISTENCE will come when beginning the six actions from Chapter 1. Unless among the two in 100 with a DEFINITE GOAL and DEFINITE PLAN, most will read the instructions and pass on without complying. He asks readers to evaluate themselves because lack of persistence is a major cause of failure, common to the majority, but overcome by effort. The ease of conquering it depends upon INTENSITY OF ONE'S DESIRE. The starting point of all achievement is DESIRE—weak desires bring weak results, as a small fire makes small heat. If lacking persistence, build a stronger fire under desires. He instructs readers to finish the chapter, return to Chapter 1, and immediately carry out the six action steps. Eagerness to follow indicates how much one really DESIRES to accumulate money. Indifference means one hasn't acquired the 'money consciousness' required. Fortunes gravitate to prepared minds as water gravitates to the ocean. If weak in PERSISTENCE, surround yourself with a MASTER MIND GROUP and develop persistence through cooperative efforts. Follow autosuggestion and subconscious mind instructions until your 'habit nature' hands over a clear picture of your DESIRE.
174: Hill explains that once the subconscious mind receives a clear picture of your DESIRE, it works continuously awake and asleep, and lack of persistence no longer handicaps you. Spasmodic or occasional effort is of no value—all rules must be applied until they become fixed habits. POVERTY is attracted to the mind favorable to it, as money is attracted to the deliberately prepared mind, through the same laws. POVERTY CONSCIOUSNESS voluntarily seizes the mind not occupied with MONEY CONSCIOUSNESS—poverty consciousness develops without conscious application, while money consciousness must be created to order. Without PERSISTENCE, you are defeated before starting; with it, you will win. Hill uses the nightmare metaphor: lying half-awake feeling about to smother, unable to move, you realize you MUST regain control. Through persistent willpower, you move fingers, then an arm, then the other arm, then legs—THEN WITH ONE SUPREME EFFORT you snap out of it, step by step. You may need to snap out of mental inertia similarly—moving slowly at first, then increasing speed until you gain complete control over your will. Be PERSISTENT no matter how slowly you move. WITH PERSISTENCE WILL COME SUCCESS. If you select your Master Mind Group with care, at least one person will aid your persistence development.
175: Hill notes some who accumulated great fortunes did so because of NECESSITY—they developed persistence because circumstances drove them. THERE IS NO SUBSTITUTE FOR PERSISTENCE—it cannot be supplanted by any other quality. Those who cultivate the HABIT of persistence enjoy insurance against failure. No matter how many times defeated, they finally arrive at the top. It appears they have a hidden Guide who tests them through discouraging experiences. Those who pick themselves up after defeat and keep trying arrive—and the world cries, 'Bravo! I knew you could do it!' The hidden Guide lets no one enjoy great achievement without passing the PERSISTENCE TEST. Those who can't take it don't make the grade. Those who can are bountifully rewarded—they receive their goal plus something infinitely more important: the knowledge that EVERY FAILURE BRINGS WITH IT THE SEED OF AN EQUIVALENT ADVANTAGE. A few know from experience the soundness of persistence—they never accept defeat as more than temporary. We see the overwhelmingly large number who go down in defeat, never to rise again, and the few who take punishment as an urge to greater effort. What we DON'T SEE is the silent but irresistible POWER coming to the rescue of those who fight on despite discouragement. If one does not possess PERSISTENCE, one does not achieve noteworthy success in any calling.
176: Hill looks up from his work to see Broadway—the 'Graveyard of Dead Hopes' and 'Front Porch of Opportunity.' People worldwide come seeking fame, fortune, power, love, or success. Occasionally someone masters Broadway, but it is not easily nor quickly conquered. Broadway acknowledges talent, recognizes genius, and pays off in money only after one has refused to QUIT. The secret of conquering Broadway is always attached to one word—PERSISTENCE! He tells the story of Fannie Hurst, who came to New York in 1915 to convert writing into riches. For four years she learned 'The Sidewalks of New York' from firsthand experience—days laboring, nights HOPING. When hope grew dim, she didn't say 'You win, Broadway' but 'You may whip some, but not me. I'm going to force you to give up.' The Saturday Evening Post sent her 36 rejection slips before she broke through. The average writer would have quit at the first rejection. Then came the payoff—publishers beat a path to her door, money came so fast she hardly had time to count it. The movie rights to her novel Great Laughter brought $100,000, said to be the highest price ever paid for a story before publication. Broadway gives any beggar coffee and a sandwich, but demands PERSISTENCE of those going after big stakes. Kate Smith would say 'Amen'—for years she sang without money before any microphone she could reach.
177: Broadway told Kate Smith, 'Come and get it, if you can take it.' She took it until Broadway got tired and said, 'Aw, what's the use? You don't know when you're whipped, so name your price.' She named her price—up in figures so high that one week's salary exceeded most people's yearly income. Hill notes THOUSANDS OF SINGERS WHOSE VOCAL SKILLS EXCEED KATE SMITH'S are walking Broadway today looking for a 'break' without success—they failed to make the grade because they lacked courage to keep on until Broadway tired of turning them away. Persistence is a state of mind, therefore cultivable. He presents 'The Eight Factors of Persistence': (1) DEFINITENESS OF PURPOSE—knowing what one wants is the first and most important step. (2) DESIRE—easy to acquire and maintain persistence when pursuing intense desire. (3) SELF-RELIANCE—belief in ability to carry out a plan. (4) DEFINITENESS OF PLANS—organized plans encourage persistence even if weak. (5) ACCURATE KNOWLEDGE—knowing plans are sound encourages persistence; guessing destroys it.
178: The Eight Factors of Persistence continue: (6) COOPERATION—sympathy, understanding, and harmonious cooperation develop persistence. (7) WILL POWER—concentrating thoughts on building plans for a definite purpose leads to persistence. (8) HABIT—persistence is the direct result of habit; the mind absorbs daily experiences; fear, the worst enemy, can be cured by forced repetition of acts of courage. Hill urges readers to inventory themselves against these eight factors. He then presents 'The 16 Symptoms of Lack of Persistence': (1) Failure to recognize and clearly define what one wants. (2) Procrastination, with or without cause, backed by alibis. (3) Lack of interest in acquiring specialized knowledge. (4) Indecision, habit of passing the buck instead of facing issues. (5) Habit of relying on alibis instead of creating definite plans.
179: The 16 Symptoms continue: (6) Self-satisfaction—little remedy, no hope for sufferers. (7) Indifference—readiness to compromise rather than meet opposition. (8) Habit of blaming others for mistakes and accepting unfavorable circumstances as unavoidable. (9) WEAKNESS OF DESIRE, from neglect in choosing MOTIVES that impel action. (10) Willingness to quit at first sign of defeat, based on one or more of the Six Basic Fears. (11) Lack of ORGANIZED PLANS in writing. (12) Habit of neglecting to act on ideas or grasp opportunity. (13) WISHING instead of WILLING. (14) Habit of compromising with POVERTY instead of aiming at riches, absence of ambition. (15) Searching for shortcuts, trying to GET without GIVING, reflected in gambling or sharp bargaining. (16) FEAR OF CRITICISM—failure to create plans and act because of what others think, say, or do. This belongs at the head of the list because it exists in the subconscious where its presence isn't recognized. Hill examines fear of criticism: the majority permit relatives, friends, and the public to influence them so they cannot live their own lives. Huge numbers make mistakes in marriage, stand by the bargain, and go through life miserable because they fear criticism. Millions neglect belated education because they fear criticism.
180: Hill continues examining the fear of criticism: countless people permit relatives to wreck their lives in the name of DUTY because they fear criticism—duty doesn't require submitting to destruction of personal ambitions. People refuse business chances because fear of criticism if they fail is stronger than DESIRE for success. Many refuse to set high goals or select a career because they fear relatives saying, 'Don't aim so high, people will think you are crazy.' Hill shares his own experience: when Andrew Carnegie suggested he devote 20 years to organizing a philosophy of individual achievement, his first impulse was fear of what people might say. His mind created alibis: 'You can't do it—the job is too big—what will relatives think?—how will you earn a living?—what right have you?—people will think you are crazy—and they did.' It seemed the whole world sought to ridicule him into giving up. Later, analyzing thousands, he discovered MOST IDEAS ARE STILLBORN AND NEED THE BREATH OF LIFE INJECTED THROUGH DEFINITE PLANS OF IMMEDIATE ACTION. The time to nurse an idea is at birth—every minute alive gives it a better chance. The FEAR OF CRITICISM is at the bottom of most ideas that never reach the PLANNING and ACTION stage.
